title: MSCI Just Added Paytm and Fortis Healthcare to Its Global Index. The Rebalancing Takes Effect Tomorrow and Could Push $2 Billion Into Indian Stocks.
excerpt: India's weight in the MSCI Global Standard index has risen to 19 per cent, its highest ever. For NRI investors watching $24 billion in foreign outflows this year, the passive money flowing back in tells a different story.
body:
Foreign portfolio investors have pulled $24 billion out of Indian stocks in 2026. The Nifty 50 is down 8.5 per cent for the year. The rupee just touched 95.90 against the dollar. By every headline measure, global money is leaving India.

And yet, as of the close of trading on May 30, a different kind of money — the kind that does not care about sentiment — is about to flow back in.

What Is Happening

MSCI, the index provider whose benchmarks are tracked by trillions of dollars in passive and institutional funds worldwide, has announced the results of its May 2026 quarterly review. The changes take effect at the close of business on May 30.

India's weight in the MSCI Global Standard index, the flagship emerging-markets benchmark, will rise to 19 per cent from 18.2 per cent. That is its highest level ever. China's weight, by contrast, will fall to 25 per cent from 25.4 per cent.

The result: India now has 149 stocks in the index, the most it has ever had. And according to estimates from Nuvama Alternative & Quantitative Research, the rebalancing is expected to drive approximately $2 billion in passive inflows into Indian equities.

Who Gets In, Who Gets Out

The headline additions to the Global Standard index include four Indian stocks:

One97 Communications (Paytm) — the fintech firm that was delisted from MSCI's mid-cap index earlier this year is being re-added to the Global Standard index. Expected passive inflows: $424 to $457 million. For a stock that traded below ₹400 in early 2024, this is a statement of rehabilitation.

Fortis Healthcare — the hospital chain is expected to attract $436 to $470 million in passive flows. India's healthcare sector has been one of the few bright spots in an otherwise difficult year for Indian equities.

GE Vernova T&D India and Siemens Energy India — two MNC subsidiaries riding the global energy transition theme.

On the exit side, Container Corporation of India (Concor) and Tata Elxsi have been removed from the index, reflecting underperformance relative to the inclusion thresholds.

In the broader May review, 13 Indian companies are being added across large-cap, mid-cap, and small-cap tiers, including JSW Energy, Canara Bank, and Indus Towers in the large-cap segment.

Why It Matters for NRI Investors

Passive flows are mechanical. When MSCI raises India's weight, every ETF and index fund tracking the benchmark must buy more Indian stocks to match. They do not wait for earnings to improve or for the rupee to stabilise. They buy because the index tells them to.

This creates a structural floor under Indian equities that is independent of the $24 billion in active selling. It does not mean the selling will stop — foreign portfolio investors have their own reasons for exiting, from elevated valuations to the AI-driven rally in US and Korean tech stocks that is pulling capital away from traditional emerging markets. India trades at more than 20 times earnings, above most major European and emerging markets, and offers one of the world's lowest dividend yields.

But it does mean that India's representation in the global investment ecosystem is growing, not shrinking. Even as active money leaves, passive money is being forced in.

For NRI investors holding Indian equities through US-listed ETFs like iShares MSCI India (INDA) or WisdomTree India Earnings (EPI), the rebalancing directly affects your portfolio. Your ETF's India allocation will adjust automatically. If you hold individual Indian stocks through an NRI demat account, the names being added — particularly Paytm and Fortis — may see short-term buying pressure around the rebalancing date.

The Bigger Picture

India's share in the MSCI Global Standard index peaked at 21 per cent in September 2024 before falling as foreign investors began their sustained exit. The recovery to 19 per cent signals that India's decline in the index was cyclical, not structural. The country's diversified economy, growing domestic investor base, and rising number of index-eligible companies are keeping it relevant in the passive investment universe.

"India is a diversified economy but Taiwan is concentrated on certain companies," SEBI chief Tuhin Kanta Pandey noted this week, after Taiwan briefly overtook India as the world's fifth-largest stock market by capitalisation. "These companies are attracting foreign flows at this time."

He is right. But the MSCI rebalancing suggests that India's problem is not relevance — it is price. When valuations normalise, and the Reuters consensus forecast expects the Nifty to recover to 26,000 by year-end, the passive infrastructure is already in place to channel money back.

The Strait of Hormuz ceasefire talks offer some additional relief. Brent crude fell to $92.6 per barrel on hopes that the US and Iran will extend their agreement, with the more actively traded August futures at $91.7. For India, which imports 80 per cent of its energy, any sustained drop in oil prices would ease the macroeconomic pressure that has been weighing on the rupee and amplifying FPI outflows.

Tomorrow's rebalancing will not reverse the $24 billion exodus. But it will remind the market that not all foreign money is discretionary — and that India's weight in the global portfolio is still rising.

Sources: MSCI Quarterly Index Review (May 2026), Nuvama Alternative & Quantitative Research, Reuters, Forbes India
